issues.title: Interval#splitBy / #divideEqually hangs forever on a negative duration (still reproducible on 3.7.2, distinct from #186)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

`Interval#splitBy(duration)` only rejects a duration whose millisecond value is *exactly* zero (`dur.as("milliseconds") === 0`). It never checks sign or finiteness. With a **negative** duration (or `divideEqually` called with a negative or `0` `numberOfParts`), the loop's cursor moves *away from* the terminal condition, so `while (s < this.e)` never becomes false. The process spins at 100%+ CPU, pushing into an ever-growing `results` array, until forcibly killed or the process runs out of memory.

This looks related to #186, but it's a different, still-open gap: the fix that closed #186 (#261) only made `Duration.fromObject({})` (an *empty* object, e.g. passing a bare `DateTime` in) return an `Invalid` Duration. A duration with real negative values, e.g. `{ hours: -1 }`, is a perfectly *valid* `Duration` and is not caught by that fix — it still hits the same non-terminating loop today.

**To Reproduce**

```js
import { Interval } from 'luxon';

// hangs forever, pins one core
Interval.fromISO('2024-01-01/2024-01-02').splitBy({ hours: -1 });

// same underlying bug via divideEqually
Interval.fromISO('2024-01-01/2024-02-01').divideEqually(-1);
Interval.fromISO('2024-01-01/2024-02-01').divideEqually(0); // length()/0 === Infinity, also never hits the ===0 guard
```

Verified against the actual `3.7.2` source (not a reimplementation): the call never returns, and `ps` shows the process pinned at 100%+ CPU with memory still climbing several seconds in:

```
$ node poc.mjs &
$ ps -o pid,pcpu,pmem,etime,comm -p <pid>
  PID  %CPU %MEM ELAPSED COMM
13063 346.8  2.8   00:06 node
```

**Actual vs Expected behavior**

Actual: the call never returns; CPU pins at 100%+; memory grows unbounded.
Expected: `splitBy`/`divideEqually` should reject/return `[]` for a non-positive or non-finite duration, the same way it already does for exactly-zero.

Suggested fix, mirroring the existing zero-check in `Interval#splitBy` (`src/interval.js`):

```js
splitBy(duration) {
  const dur = Duration.fromDurationLike(duration);
  const ms = dur.as("milliseconds");

  if (!this.isValid || !dur.isValid || !Number.isFinite(ms) || ms <= 0) {
    return [];
  }
  ...
```

and validating `numberOfParts` is a finite integer `>= 1` in `divideEqually` before delegating to `splitBy`. A loop-progress assertion (e.g. `if (+next <= +s) break;`) would also be reasonable defense-in-depth.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- OS: Linux/macOS (platform-independent — pure JS loop)
- Luxon version: 3.7.2 (current latest at time of testing; verified against source at GitHub tag `3.7.2`)
- Node: v24.16.0 (reproduces on any Node in luxon's supported range)

**Additional context**

Since a single request-supplied negative duration or non-positive part count can wedge Node's single-threaded event loop for the whole process (not just the caller's own request), this has denial-of-service implications for any server-side code that forwards a request-derived duration/part-count into `splitBy`/`divideEqually` (e.g. scheduling/billing/calendar-slicing endpoints). Happy to open a PR with the one-line fix above if that's useful.
issues.author: manqingzhou

issues.title: Interval#isEmpty() throws TypeError on an Invalid interval instead of returning false (unlike its siblings)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

`Interval#isEmpty()` reads `this.s.valueOf()` directly with no `isValid` guard — unlike its siblings `isAfter`, `isBefore`, `contains`, and `engulfs`, which all start with `if (!this.isValid) return false;`. On an `Invalid` `Interval` (e.g. produced by an end-before-start range, or `Interval.invalid(...)`), `this.s` is `undefined`, so `isEmpty()` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'valueOf')` instead of returning a boolean — breaking the "Invalid objects don't throw" contract the rest of the `Interval` API follows.

**To Reproduce**

```js
import { Interval } from 'luxon';

const iv = Interval.fromISO('2024-06-01T12:00Z/2024-06-01T06:00Z'); // end < start -> Invalid
console.log(iv.isValid); // false
iv.isEmpty(); // throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'valueOf')

Interval.invalid('whatever').isEmpty(); // throws the same way
```

Verified against the actual `3.7.2` source; both calls throw as described.

**Actual vs Expected behavior**

Actual: `isEmpty()` throws an uncaught `TypeError` on any `Invalid` interval.
Expected: like its siblings, it should return `false` for an `Invalid` interval instead of throwing.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- Luxon version: 3.7.2 (current latest; verified against source at GitHub tag `3.7.2`)
- Node: v24.16.0

**Additional context**

Suggested fix — a one-line guard matching the pattern already used four times elsewhere in `src/interval.js`:

```js
isEmpty() {
  if (!this.isValid) return false;
  return this.s.valueOf() === this.e.valueOf();
}
```

Might be worth a quick audit of the other `Interval`/`DateTime`/`Duration` instance methods for the same unguarded-`this.s`/`this.e` pattern, and/or a small generated test that calls every public method on `Interval.invalid("test")` and asserts none of them throw.
issues.author: manqingzhou

issues.title: Duration.fromISO("P"/"PT"/"-P") parses as a valid zero duration, causing Interval overlaps()/merge() to silently ignore the interval
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

`luxon`'s ISO-8601 duration regex (`isoDuration` in `src/impl/regexParser.js`) makes every component group optional, including the whole `T` clause. That means the bare strings `"P"`, `"PT"`, and `"-P"` — none of which specify any actual duration component, and none of which are valid ISO 8601 (which requires at least one designator) — match the grammar. `extractISODuration` then returns an object whose fields are all `undefined`, which is still *truthy*, so `Duration.fromISO` treats it as a successful parse and normalizes it to a valid zero-length `Duration`.

Fed into `Interval.fromISO("<start>/P")` (a standard, documented interval-string form), this produces a *structurally valid*, zero-length interval — `isValid: true`. Since `isValid` is the library's own documented guard for "is this safe to use," and it doesn't fire here, `overlaps()`/`merge()`/`contains()` silently treat this interval as a no-op: a "blackout"/deny/maintenance window expressed as `"<start>/P"` reports no overlap with anything, and `merge()` drops it entirely.

**To Reproduce**

```js
import { Duration, Interval } from 'luxon';

console.log(Duration.fromISO('P').isValid);   // true (should be false)
console.log(Duration.fromISO('PT').isValid);  // true
console.log(Duration.fromISO('-P').isValid);  // true

const maintenance = Interval.fromISO('2024-06-01T09:00Z/P');
console.log(maintenance.isValid, maintenance.isEmpty()); // true true

const booking = Interval.fromISO('2024-06-01T09:00Z/2024-06-01T10:00Z');
console.log(maintenance.overlaps(booking));               // false — no conflict detected
console.log(Interval.merge([maintenance, booking]).length); // 1 — maintenance window silently dropped
```

Verified against the actual `3.7.2` source; output matches exactly.

**Actual vs Expected behavior**

Actual: `"P"`/`"PT"`/`"-P"` parse as valid zero durations; an interval built from one is `isValid: true` and silently disappears from `overlaps`/`merge` checks.
Expected: per ISO 8601, a duration must specify at least one component — `Duration.fromISO("P")` (and `"PT"`/`"-P"`) should produce an `Invalid` Duration.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- Luxon version: 3.7.2 (current latest; verified against source at GitHub tag `3.7.2`)
- Node: v24.16.0

**Additional context**

Suggested fix: in `extractISODuration`, detect the "every capture group is `undefined`" case and return `[null]` instead, so these strings become `Invalid` Durations. Given some callers may legitimately want zero-length intervals to be representable, it's probably not right to change `Interval.fromDateTimes` itself — but it would help to document (or provide an explicit `conflictsWith()`/strict variant of `overlaps`) that `isEmpty()` intervals need special handling in any deny/window-conflict logic, since the current behavior is easy to miss (an `Interval` can be simultaneously `isValid: true` and `isEmpty(): true`, and none of `overlaps`/`contains`/`engulfs`/`merge` special-case that).
issues.author: manqingzhou

issues.title: fullwide/hanidec numberingSystem: digit matcher and decoder tables have drifted apart, causing silent data corruption
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

`src/impl/digits.js` keeps two independently-authored representations per numbering system: a regex character class used to *recognize* a digit, and a code-point range/char array used to *decode* it. Two of these have drifted out of sync, and `parseDigits()` has no fail-closed branch, so a recognized-but-undecodable character silently corrupts the parsed value while the resulting `DateTime`/`Duration` still reports `isValid: true`:

1. **`fullwide` off-by-two.** The matcher `[０-９]` accepts U+FF10–U+FF19 (all ten full-width digits), but the decoder range `numberingSystemsUTF16.fullwide` is `[65296, 65303]` (only up to U+FF17). Full-width `８`/`９` (U+FF18/U+FF19) match as digits but decode to nothing — they're silently dropped from the accumulator.
2. **Literal `|` inside the `hanidec` character class.** The source string `"[〇|一|二|三|四|五|六|七|八|九]"` puts a literal `|` inside a character class (where it has no alternation meaning), so the compiled regex matches an ordinary pipe as a "digit." Meanwhile `hanidecChars` strips `|` when building the decode array, so `hanidecChars.indexOf("|")` returns `-1`, and `value += -1` string-concatenates a literal `"-1"` into the parsed number.

**To Reproduce**

```js
import { DateTime } from 'luxon';

const dt1 = DateTime.fromFormat('２０１８-０１-０１', 'yyyy-MM-dd', { numberingSystem: 'fullwide' });
console.log(dt1.year, dt1.isValid); // -> 201 true  (should be 2018, or Invalid)

const dt2 = DateTime.fromFormat('|', 'y', { numberingSystem: 'hanidec' });
console.log(dt2.year, dt2.isValid); // -> -1 true
```

Verified against the actual `3.7.2` source; output matches exactly.

**Actual vs Expected behavior**

Actual: `２０１８` parses to year `201` (the full-width `8` vanishes); a lone `|` parses to `-1` — both report `isValid: true` with no `invalidReason`.
Expected: either these characters decode correctly, or the parse should fail (`isValid: false`) rather than silently emitting a value the input never contained.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- Luxon version: 3.7.2 (current latest; verified against source at GitHub tag `3.7.2`)
- Node: v24.16.0

**Additional context**

Suggested fix:
- Correct the `fullwide` decoder range to `[65296, 65305]`.
- Remove the literal pipes from the `hanidec` character class: `"[〇一二三四五六七八九]"`.
- Make `parseDigits` fail closed: if a matched character can't be resolved by any decoder table (or resolves to `indexOf`'s `-1` sentinel), return `NaN` for the whole parse instead of silently dropping/misinterpreting the character.
- A regression test round-tripping all ten digits for every supported `numberingSystem`, plus explicit rejection tests for `|`/`[`/`]` under `hanidec`, would catch regressions here.
issues.author: manqingzhou

issues.title: `Interval#overlaps` returns true for an empty interval inside another interval
issues.body:
On current master, an empty interval strictly inside a non-empty interval reports an overlap, while the same empty interval at either endpoint does not. This disagrees with `intersection()` and with the zero-length half-open semantics discussed in #1188.

Luxon: master @ f427515 (after 3.7.2); timezone irrelevant (UTC).

```js
const { DateTime, Interval } = require('luxon');
const dt = (hour) => DateTime.utc(2026, 1, 1, hour);
const interval = Interval.fromDateTimes(dt(5), dt(8));
const empty = Interval.fromDateTimes(dt(6), dt(6));
console.log(interval.overlaps(empty)); // true
console.log(empty.overlaps(interval)); // true
console.log(interval.intersection(empty)); // null
console.log(empty.contains(dt(6))); // false
```

Expected: both overlap checks return false. Empty intervals contain no instants regardless of their position.

I have a small fix with regression tests: `overlaps()` requires both intervals to have positive length. Would you accept a fix for this? It would also mean `Interval.merge()` drops isolated empty intervals (and returns `[]` for all-empty input) — see #1807 for a related, opposite concern.

Reproduced on master (f427515), Node 24.21.0. AI assistance was used for this report, which I reviewed myself.

issues.title: Constructing IANAZones has huge memory impact on nodejs
issues.body:
I have not dug deep enough to really get to the bottom of the issue here but this should serve as a warning to all that use Luxon on nodejs along with timezones. I have an algorithm that uses timezones in its core loop. The first version reads like this:
```ts
const zone = new IANAZone(asset.timezone);
const assetHour = data.date.setZone(zone);
if (assetHour.hour !== 23) { return; }
```
which produced the following memory graph on the server (two instances running, scale is in MB)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4698832/115369477-6da51a80-a1c8-11eb-8e6a-16702489a234.png)
So each run consumed roughly 1Gb of memory that could not be freed and eventually destabilized the whole stack.
The new version that avoids using instances of `IANAZone` seems to avoid a crucial memory issue somewhere hidden in the `IANAZone` constructor or in the calls to `setZone`:
```ts
const assetHour = data.date.setZone(asset.timezone);
if (assetHour.hour !== 23) { return; }
```
This version does not consume any noteworthy memory anymore. After redeployment at `10:45` note the small bump at `10:55` that belongs to the invocation.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4698832/115370381-4dc22680-a1c9-11eb-80ae-feb4cffeb52b.png)
I find this stunning how two tiny seemingly equivalent pieces code can have such a huge difference in memory consumption.
issues.author: sechel

comments.body: Yeah, the Intl API is just brutal in v8, both in terms of memory and CPU. We cache the Intl objects we create because it's so slow, which is why the memory is ratcheting up. The best I can offer is that we could add the ability to control the cache, at least on/off.
comments.author: icambron

comments.body:
If I understand this correctly, the difference between the two pieces of code is that the first one uses the `IANAZone` constructor directly. The 2nd piece of code still uses `IANAZone` indirectly via `setZone`, but that uses `IANAZone.create`, which implements the cache.
As such the problem doesn't even seem to be the Intl API in this case but just the sheer number of `IANAZone` instances.
The `IANAZone` constructor should be deprecated and marked private in favor of the caching factory function, just like other classes in Luxon behave.

manqingzhou

issues.title: DateTime.fromFormat on the DST switch day
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
Using DateTime.fromFormat('02:30', 'hh:mm') returns an unexpectedly valid result even if it is not when doing it on the day of DST change (2026-03-29 in Europe e.g.) for a time to parse that just doesn't exist. Instead it silently shifts the hour by the difference of the zone offset.

**To Reproduce**
DateTime.fromFormat('02:30', 'hh:mm').isValid
returns true when executed in Europe/Berlin timezone on 2026-03-29.
DateTime.fromFormat('02:30', 'hh:mm').hour
returns 3

**Actual vs Expected behavior**
DateTime.fromFormat('02:30', 'hh:mm').isValid
should return false when executed in Europe/Berlin timezone on 2026-03-29.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04
- Browser: irrelevant
- Luxon version: 3.7.2
- Your timezone: Europe/Berlin

**Additional context**
nothing to add here
issues.author: john30

comments.body:
@john30 I was curious what the behavior looked like in other librarys, so I fed the same date into date-fns and got this:

```
const { DateTime } = require("luxon");
const l = DateTime.fromObject({
    year: 2026,
    month: 3,
    day: 29,
    hour: 2,
    minute: 30,
}, {
    zone: "Europe/Stockholm"
})
console.log("Luxon")
console.log(`Valid: ${l.isValid}`)
console.log(`Time: ${l.hour}:${l.minute}`)

const {TZDate} = require("@date-fns/tz")
const d = new TZDate("2026-03-29 02:30:00", "Europe/Stockholm")
console.log("date-fns")
console.log(`Time: ${d.getHours()}:${d.getMinutes()}`)
```

```
% yarn start
Luxon
Valid: true
Time: 3:30
date-fns
Time: 3:30
```

issues.title: fromFormat and unix epoch
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
I cannot use the token 'x' and 'X' to convert a unix epoch time in (milli)seconds to a datetime using the .fromFormat() method.

**To Reproduce**
`luxon.DateTime.fromFormat('1769758221', 'X')`

**Actual vs Expected behavior**
fromFormat() method gives a unparseable error with explanation _the input "1769758221" can't be parsed as format X_ .
I expect the result to be datetime object which when converted toISO() is _2026-01-30T08:30:21.000+01:00_

**Desktop:**

- OS: Windows 11
- Browser Chrome 144.0.7559.97
- Luxon version 3.7.2
- Europe/Amsterdam

**Additional context**
I may be misunderstanding if fromFormat() method can convert from unix epoch timestamps at all. It is not clear from the documentation. There is a macro token 'x' and 'X' but it seems to work for the toFormat() method instead.
issues.author: nlooije

comments.body:
The tokens for fromFormat and toFormat are different (see the different tables for [formatting](https://moment.github.io/luxon/#/formatting?id=table-of-tokens) and [parsing](https://moment.github.io/luxon/#/parsing?id=table-of-tokens)). They align in many places, but not everything that can be formatted can also be parsed, due to ambiguities or lack of browser APIs. For example, you can format a time zone as a short string ("EST" for example), but the resulting string is ambiguous, so there is no parsing token for it.
"X" and "x" are formatting tokens, but not parsing tokens. It should be easy to add the parsing tokens, but I wouldn't take this as a high priority issue, because you can use `fromMillis` and `fromSeconds`.
